body.hook: Some of the most powerful moments in theatre have no words at all: a group moving together like a single wave, a crowd freezing in shock, a line of people slowly turning away from one person. When an ensemble moves as one, the audience feels it.

study.title: Moving as One
study.question: How does an ensemble use movement to express a theme?
study.passage:
Warm-up, Flocking (8 minutes): Groups of five stand in a diamond, all facing the same way. The person at the front leads slow movements; everyone follows. When the leader turns, the new person at the front becomes the leader.
Skill builder (10 minutes): Practise three techniques:
• Unison: all perform a gesture together on a count of 8.
• Canon: the same gesture rippling down a line.
• Contrast: one person moves slowly while everyone else moves quickly, or one person stays still while others move.
Creation (20 minutes): Each group creates a 60–90 second movement piece on one theme: "the storm," "rush hour," "belonging," "the last day of school" or "change." Requirements: a clear opening and ending tableau, at least one unison section, one canon section, one moment of contrast that directs focus, and smooth transitions. Music without lyrics may be used.
Share and feedback (10 minutes): Groups perform. Audience gives one "glow" (strength) and one "grow" (suggestion), naming where their focus went.

body.objective: Students will be able to use focus and contrast in movement.

body.hook: In a room full of moving bodies, how does an audience know where to look? Choreographers and directors control focus the same way painters do: through contrast. One still figure among moving ones, one high body among low ones, and every eye goes there.

vocabulary.definition: Where the audience's attention is directed.
A strong difference, such as fast and slow or high and low.
Performers moving the same way at the same time.
Performers doing the same movement one after another.
Not moving, often used to draw focus.
The paths and shapes performers make across the space.

study.title: Where Do We Look?
study.question: How do contrast and focus make an ensemble piece clear?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Find the focus (10 minutes): Half the class moves around the space; one person is told secretly to create focus without leaving the group. Observers guess who it is and how they did it (stopping, changing level, moving slowly, facing a different way).
2. Contrast pairs (10 minutes): Groups of five try: all fast + one slow; all low + one high; all facing upstage + one facing the audience; unison + one breaking away.
3. Unison and canon (5 minutes): Learn an eight-count movement phrase. Perform it in unison, then in canon (each person starts two counts later).
4. Apply (20 minutes): Revisit your ensemble movement piece on your theme (from the last lesson). Add at least two moments of deliberate focus using contrast, one unison section and one canon section. Decide why each moment of focus matters to your theme.

body.objective: Students will be able to refine a piece with feedback.
body.iCan: I can refine a piece with feedback.
successCriteria: I can give specific feedback on movement pieces
I can use feedback to refine timing, transitions and clarity
I can perform a polished ensemble piece
body.hook: Choreographers rarely finish a piece in one try. They watch, cut, adjust timing and try again. The difference between a good movement piece and a great one is usually refinement.

vocabulary.definition: To make small improvements that polish a piece.
How performers move from one section to the next.
When movements happen in relation to counts, music or each other.

A set structure for giving and receiving feedback.

study.title: Polish the Piece
study.question: How does feedback help an ensemble refine its work?
study.passage:
Feedback protocol (written for this lesson):
1. Perform: Each group runs its piece once for another group.
2. Warm feedback (1 minute): Observers say what was clear and powerful: "The canon section looked like a wave of fear."
3. Cool feedback (1 minute): Observers say what was unclear, using questions: "What was happening in the middle section?" "Were the performers meant to be in unison at the end?"
4. Performers listen without defending.
5. Refine (20 minutes): Choose three changes. Common refinements: clean up unison so counts match; smooth transitions so there's no "dead" moment; hold stillness longer; make the beginning and ending shapes clearer; cut anything that doesn't support the theme.
6. Final performance with a clear start (performers in a starting shape, stillness) and a clear ending (a final shape held for three counts).
